paragraphs: It is explained in the Gemara and in the poskim that since wine is significant enough to require its own berachah — that one recites "Borei peri hagafen" over it in several places, such as Kiddush, Havdalah, Birkat HaMazon, the night of Pesach, betrothal, marriage, and circumcision — even though one does not need to drink it and is not craving it, it is therefore not considered secondary to bread so as to be exempted by the first berachah, which is Borei peri hagafen, even though it is secondary to bread with respect to being exempted by Birkat HaMazon from the concluding berachah. This is because wine does not require its own concluding berachah, only its own opening berachah, which is the main reason the cup is brought in all the aforementioned matters that require a cup. Therefore, even though the wine is drunk during the meal, one recites Borei peri hagafen over it, and it is not exempted by the berachah on bread — even though one drinks it in order to soak the food in one's stomach, which would otherwise make it like other things that come on account of the meal during the meal and are exempted along with the bread. Nevertheless, since wine is significant enough to require its own berachah in the several places mentioned above, even though one does not need to drink it, as we have explained, it is therefore not secondary to bread — unlike other foods and drinks that come during the meal on account of the meal, which are secondary to the bread and do not require a berachah, as we shall explain, please God. All of this is explicitly stated in the Shulchan Aruch of the Gaon Rabbeinu Zalman, siman 174, se'if 1.

clarification.explanation: Wine is especially significant in that it generates its own berachah (Borei peri hagafen) in a number of places — Kiddush, Havdalah, Birkat HaMazon, the night of Pesach, betrothal and marriage, and circumcision — even though one does not need to drink it and does not crave it. Therefore wine is not considered secondary to bread and is not exempted by the berachah of Hamotzi (the opening berachah), even though it is exempted by the concluding berachah (Birkat HaMazon), because wine does not generate its own concluding berachah — only its own opening berachah, for whose sake the cup is brought in all those matters. Therefore, even if one drinks wine during the meal, one recites Borei peri hagafen over it, and it is not exempted by the berachah on bread — unlike other foods and drinks that come on account of the meal, which are exempted by the berachah on bread.
takeaways: One recites Borei peri hagafen over wine on its own even during the meal, because it "generates its own berachah" (at Kiddush, Havdalah, etc.).
Only its opening berachah stands on its own; its concluding berachah is indeed exempted by Birkat HaMazon.

paragraphs: Wine gained a further distinction and virtue: it exempts all types of beverages. Therefore, if one recited a berachah over wine, one need not recite a berachah over other beverages, for wine exempts all types of beverages, whether during the meal or at other times, because wine is the primary beverage and the head of all types of beverages, and therefore it is primary with respect to the berachah, and all others are secondary to it. This applies provided the beverages are before him at the time he recites the berachah over the wine, or that he has them in mind. And even if he does not set himself to drink wine, but drinks a small amount of wine casually for the sake of a mitzvah or the like, and afterward drinks many other beverages — they are exempted by the berachah on the wine if he had them in mind; but if he did not set himself to drink but merely drinks a little casually and did not have other beverages in mind, they are not exempted by the berachah on the wine.

Therefore one must be careful, when reciting Kiddush on Shabbat over wine, that if he wishes to drink water or other beverages after Kiddush and before the berachah of Hamotzi, the water must be before him or he must have it in mind, and then he need not recite a berachah over the water or other beverages. It is also proper to caution one who drinks water between Kiddush and Hamotzi not to drink a revi'it, so that he not become obligated in a concluding berachah and thereby enter the confusion of the dispute — for there are those who say that he must recite a concluding berachah, since Birkat HaMazon does not exempt the water he drank before Hamotzi, and there are those who say he need not recite one. Therefore it is good to be careful not to drink a revi'it. However, if he erred and drank a revi'it, he should recite a concluding berachah over the water before Hamotzi, for although there are those who disagree, nevertheless this view is primary, because such was the ruling of our great teacher the Ari, may his memory be blessed, who perceived with divine inspiration on the forehead of our teacher Rabbi Chaim Vital, may his memory be blessed, on one occasion that he had drunk a revi'it of water before Birkat HaMazon and had not recited a concluding berachah, and he rebuked him about this, as mentioned in Sha'ar Ta'amei HaMitzvot, Parashat Eikev — see there. And even though this incident involving our teacher Rabbi Chaim Vital, may his memory be blessed, brought in the aforementioned Sha'ar Ta'amei HaMitzvot, may possibly have occurred on a weekday, nevertheless it appears that the same law applies to a Shabbat meal that includes Kiddush, according to the view of our great teacher the Ari, may his memory be blessed, as I have proven and clarified in my sacred work Makabtzi'el, please God. See also Rav Birkei Yosef, siman 174, se'if katan 2 — see there.

clarification.explanation:
Wine has an additional virtue: it exempts all other types of beverages. Therefore, one who recites a berachah over wine need not recite a berachah over other beverages (whether during the meal or not at the time of a meal), because wine is the primary beverage and all other beverages are secondary to it. The condition for this: the other beverages must be before him at the time of the berachah over the wine, or he must intend them explicitly. Even one who does not set himself to drink wine, but drinks a little wine casually (for example, for the sake of a mitzvah), and afterward drinks a great deal of other beverages — those beverages are exempted by the berachah on the wine if he intended them; but if he did not set himself to drink and did not intend the other beverages, they are not exempted.
Therefore, one who recites Kiddush over wine on Shabbat and wishes afterward to drink water or another beverage before the berachah of Hamotzi must have the water before him at the time of the berachah on the wine, or intend it, and then he need not recite a separate berachah over it. It is also good to be careful not to drink a revi'it of water between Kiddush and Hamotzi, so as not to enter into doubt as to whether one is obligated in a concluding berachah over that water (there is a dispute: some say one is obligated, since Birkat HaMazon does not exempt it, and some say one is not obligated). And if one nevertheless erred and drank a revi'it of water before Hamotzi, he should recite a concluding berachah over it (Borei nefashot rabbot) before Hamotzi — for such is the ruling of our teacher the Ari, may his memory be blessed: it is told that the Ari perceived with divine inspiration that his disciple Rabbeinu Chaim Vital had once drunk a revi'it of water before Birkat HaMazon without reciting a concluding berachah, and rebuked him for this. The Ben Ish Chai explains that this law applies also to a Shabbat meal that includes Kiddush, and not only on a weekday.
takeaways: The berachah on wine exempts all other beverages, provided they are before him at the time of the berachah or he intends them.
At Shabbat Kiddush, if one wishes to drink water before Hamotzi, it is best to intend it in the berachah on the wine, and to avoid drinking a full revi'it so as not to enter into doubt.
If one nevertheless drank a revi'it of water before Hamotzi, he recites a concluding berachah over it, as the Ari, may his memory be blessed, instructed.

paragraphs: Wine drunk before the meal, such as the Kiddush recited in place of a meal, exempts the wine drunk during the meal, if he had it in mind to drink during the meal. But if it is not his custom to do so and he changes his mind and wishes to drink, or others gave it to him, he must recite the berachah again.

clarification.explanation: Wine drunk before the meal (such as Kiddush recited in place of a meal) also exempts wine drunk during the meal, if he had intended to drink it during the meal. But if it is not his usual practice and he changes his mind and wishes to drink, or others served it to him, he must recite the berachah again.
takeaways: Kiddush exempts additional wine drunk during the meal — only if he intended so beforehand.
Changing his mind without prior intent, or receiving wine from others — he must recite the berachah again.

paragraphs: One should not recite a concluding berachah over the wine of Kiddush that is in place of a meal, or over wine drunk before the rest of the meal, at whatever time it may be — even if he does not drink wine during the meal — because Birkat HaMazon exempts the concluding berachah of the wine drunk before the meal. But if he ate mezonot foods before the berachah of Hamotzi, he should recite a berachah me'ein shalosh before the netilat yadayim that precedes Hamotzi, and should not rely on Birkat HaMazon from the outset. And if he did not recite a concluding berachah before Hamotzi and remembered only after having recited Hamotzi, he should not recite a concluding berachah over the mezonot foods he ate before Hamotzi, but should only intend to exempt them through Birkat HaMazon.

And all this applies specifically to mezonot foods; but if he ate fruits or drank beverages before the berachah of Hamotzi and forgot and did not recite a concluding berachah before netilat yadayim and Hamotzi, and remembered after the berachah of Hamotzi, he should recite a concluding berachah even in the middle of the meal, because Birkat HaMazon exempts only things that come within the meal itself — see the acharonim.

clarification.explanation: One does not recite a concluding berachah over the wine of Kiddush (which comes in place of a meal) or over wine drunk before the meal, because Birkat HaMazon exempts it. But if he ate mezonot foods (cake and the like) before Hamotzi, he should recite a berachah me'ein shalosh before netilat yadayim, and should not rely on Birkat HaMazon from the outset; and if he forgot and remembered only after Hamotzi, he should no longer recite a berachah, but should intend to exempt them through Birkat HaMazon. But fruits and beverages eaten or drunk before Hamotzi that he forgot to recite a concluding berachah over — if he remembers after Hamotzi, he recites a concluding berachah over them even in the middle of the meal, because Birkat HaMazon exempts only things that are within the meal itself.
takeaways: Kiddush wine and mezonot foods that were forgotten — are exempted by Birkat HaMazon.
Fruits/beverages forgotten before Hamotzi — one recites a concluding berachah over them even in the middle of the meal.

paragraphs: If one drinks water during the meal, there are those who say one recites a berachah over it, and there are those who say one does not recite a berachah, and we hold that in cases of doubt regarding berachot we are lenient, so one should not recite the berachah, but should merely contemplate the berachah in his heart, or say "Blessed is the Merciful One, by Whose word all things came to be." Therefore, in order to remove oneself from this doubt that exists among the poskim, one should sit before netilah in the place of the meal and drink water and recite a berachah over it with the intent of exempting everything he will drink during his meal. However, he must be careful to drink less than the required measure, so that he not become obligated in a concluding berachah — for if he recites a concluding berachah, his remedy will have accomplished nothing, since he will then be unable to exempt with that berachah what he drinks during the meal. He must also be careful not to go outside after drinking, because one who changes his place must recite the berachah again upon returning to his place, and thus his remedy would have accomplished nothing. And so wrote our teacher Rabbi Chaim Vital, may his memory be blessed, regarding this remedy of drinking water, and he cautioned that one should drink less than the required measure so as not to become obligated in a concluding berachah. And if there is wine at the meal, none of this is necessary, because the berachah on wine exempts all types of beverages, as mentioned in Sha'ar Ta'amei HaMitzvot.

Now, this remedy of drinking water before Hamotzi cannot be done at all times, because sometimes a person is not at all thirsty for water before Hamotzi, and whenever one is not thirsty and has no craving for water at all, there is room to doubt whether it is permitted to do so and recite a berachah over it. And although there are those who explicitly permit this — that he recites the berachah in order to exempt the water drunk during the meal — nevertheless the matter is not clear to us, and one should not place himself in doubt regarding berachot. See Chesed LaAlafim, siman 174, ot 4, in the gloss of "Mar breih deRavina," may his memory be blessed — see there. Therefore, if he is not thirsty and has no craving for water at all, or if he has already washed his hands and did not perform the aforementioned remedy of drinking water, he should be careful to recite Shehakol over a piece of sugar or the like during the meal before drinking the water, and intend to exempt the water he will drink. And such was the custom of the crown of our heads, my father the Rav, may the memory of the righteous be for a blessing, to recite a berachah over sweet foods always before drinking water during the meal, and he was very careful about this. Therefore every person is right to be careful about this. However, at the two Shabbat meals at which one recites Kiddush over wine, one need not be careful about all this, because the berachah on the Kiddush wine, which is in place of a meal, exempts all beverages during the meal, and one must intend, in the berachah on the wine, to exempt the water during the meal. See Tzapichit BiDvash, siman 6 — see there. And there are those who are precise to say, before Kiddush on Shabbat, after saying "L'shem yichud," etc., "And behold I intend to exempt, with the berachah I will recite over the wine of Kiddush, all types of beverages that I will drink during the meal." This custom is correct, because a person is prone to forgetfulness, and thereby he is found to be diligent and rewarded.

clarification.explanation:
One who drinks water during the meal — there are those who say he recites a berachah over it, and those who say he does not; and since in doubtful cases regarding berachot we are lenient, he should not recite a berachah, but should contemplate the berachah in his heart or say "Blessed is the Merciful One, by Whose word all things came to be." To remove himself from this doubt, he should sit before netilat yadayim in the place of the meal, drink water, and recite a berachah over it with the intent of exempting everything he will drink during the meal; but he must be careful to drink less than the required measure, so as not to become obligated in a concluding berachah (for if he recites a concluding berachah, the remedy is nullified), and not to go outside afterward (since one who changes his place must recite the berachah again). So wrote Rav Chaim Vital, may his memory be blessed. And if there is wine at the meal, none of this is necessary, since the berachah on wine exempts all beverages.
However, this remedy (drinking water before Hamotzi) is not always possible, since sometimes one is not thirsty at all; and one who is not thirsty should doubt whether it is permitted for him to recite a berachah over the water, and one should not place oneself in doubt. Therefore, if he is not thirsty, or has already washed his hands and did not perform the remedy, he should recite Shehakol over a piece of sugar or the like during the meal before drinking, and intend to exempt the water (and such was the custom of the Ben Ish Chai's father, to be very careful about this). And at the two Shabbat meals at which one recites Kiddush over wine, none of this is necessary, since the berachah on the Kiddush wine (which is in place of a meal) exempts all beverages; and he should intend in it to exempt the water. And there are those who are precise to say this explicitly before Kiddush — and this is a proper custom, since a person is prone to forget.
takeaways: Water during the meal — it is doubtful whether one recites a berachah over it, and doubtful berachot are treated leniently; one should not recite a berachah but should contemplate it or say "Blessed is the Merciful One, by Whose word all things came to be."

Remedy: drink water before netilat yadayim and recite a berachah with intent to exempt (less than the required measure, and without going outside afterward); and if not thirsty — recite Shehakol over sugar to exempt.
At Kiddush over wine — the berachah on the wine exempts the water; one should intend this in it (and some are accustomed to say this explicitly).

paragraphs: Regarding beer drunk during the meal: if one drinks it to arouse appetite for food, it is secondary to the meal and one need not recite a berachah over it; and if one drinks it to warm the stomach in order to digest the food, one must recite a berachah over it. However, since often one will find that a person's intent is to arouse his appetite for food, it is difficult to determine the drinker's intent with certainty, and for the most part he intends both purposes, and we hold that in cases of doubt regarding berachot we are lenient — therefore he should not recite a berachah over it. Moreover, apart from this, the berachah over beer is not clear to everyone, because it burns the throat, and there are people for whom it is like a painful thorn, and because of this they are accustomed to drink water immediately afterward. Therefore it is good to be careful to eat something whose berachah is Shehakol, such as sugar and the like, before drinking the beer, and to intend to exempt the beer. And the Rav my father, may the memory of the righteous be for a blessing, is remembered for good, for he never in his life recited a berachah over beer, but would take a piece of sugar and recite a berachah to exempt it. And even when he drank a small cup of beer during the day for some purpose that was not at the time of a meal, his practice was to recite the berachah first over a piece of sugar, since he kept one ready for this purpose. And we have already said that at the Shabbat and Yom Tov meals at which one recites Kiddush over wine, one need not perform this remedy, because the berachah on the Kiddush wine exempts all beverages; therefore one should intend by it to exempt water, beer, and all types of beverages.

clarification.explanation: Beer (an intoxicating beverage) drunk during the meal: if one drinks it to arouse appetite — it is secondary to the meal and one does not recite a berachah over it; and if one drinks it to warm the stomach and digest the food — one must recite a berachah. But since it is difficult to know clearly the drinker's intent (usually both intentions are mixed together), the halachah follows the principle that in doubtful cases regarding berachot we are lenient — so one should not recite a berachah over it alone. Therefore it is good to eat something whose berachah is Shehakol (such as sugar) before drinking the beer and intend to exempt it; and at Shabbat/Yom Tov meals with Kiddush over wine — this is not necessary, since the berachah on the wine exempts everything. This advice is correct not only during the meal: the Ben Ish Chai testifies that his father, may his memory be blessed, always practiced this — even when he drank a small cup of beer during the day for some purpose not at the time of a meal at all, he would recite a berachah first over a piece of sugar that he kept ready for this purpose, and thereby exempt the beer.
takeaways: Beer during the meal — a doubtful berachah, therefore one does not recite a berachah over it alone.
One exempts it with the berachah of Shehakol over sugar beforehand, or with the berachah on the Kiddush wine.
The practice of reciting Shehakol over sugar before beer is good to follow even not at the time of a meal — every time one drinks a cup of beer during the day.

paragraphs: Things that come during the meal: if they come on account of the meal — that is, they are things one customarily makes a meal upon — whether they come to be eaten with the bread as a relish, such as meat, fish, vegetables, cheese, eggs, and types of salted foods, or whether they come to nourish and satiate, such as types of cooked dishes made in a pot, which do not come to be eaten with the bread as a relish but to nourish and satiate — these do not require a berachah before them even if one eats them without bread, because the berachah of Hamotzi exempts them, and they do not require a berachah after them, because Birkat HaMazon exempts them, since it is not the custom to eat these all day long like fruits, but only at the time of a meal; therefore they are secondary to the bread, which is the essence of the meal, and are exempted by the berachah on the bread even though one eats them without bread. And all types of fruits that come during the meal — if one eats them with bread, no berachah at all is required, because since he now eats them with the bread they have become secondary to the bread, and the berachah of Hamotzi exempts them. But if one does not eat them with bread but eats them alone at the end of the meal for dessert and mere enjoyment, these require a berachah before them and are not exempted by the berachah of Hamotzi, since they are not part of the essence of the meal and are customarily eaten all day even not at the time of a meal. But they do not require a berachah after them, because since they came during the meal before one's hands were withdrawn from the bread, Birkat HaMazon exempts them, for everything that comes during the meal is included in the satiety of which it is said, "And you shall eat and be satisfied and bless," as is written in the Shulchan Aruch of the Gaon Rabbeinu Zalman, may his memory be blessed.

clarification.explanation: Foods that come during the meal on account of the meal — whether those eaten as a relish with the bread (meat, fish, vegetables, cheese, eggs, salted foods) or those that come to nourish and satiate (cooked pot dishes) — do not require a berachah before or after them, even if eaten without bread, because the berachah of Hamotzi and Birkat HaMazon exempt them (since they are customarily eaten only at the time of a meal, unlike fruits eaten all day). Likewise, fruits eaten with the bread do not require a berachah, since they have become secondary to the bread; but if eaten alone at the end of the meal for dessert and enjoyment, they require an opening berachah (since they are not part of the essence of the meal and are also eaten not at the time of a meal), but they do not require a concluding berachah, since everything that comes during the meal is included in the satiety that Birkat HaMazon exempts.
takeaways: Foods that serve as a relish for bread or that satiate — are exempt from a berachah (even without bread).
Fruits eaten separately for dessert — require an opening berachah, but not a concluding one (Birkat HaMazon exempts it).

paragraphs: If one made something other than fruit the basis of his meal, and fruits were also brought before him, and he eats some of them with bread and some without bread, there are differing views on this matter: some say that as long as he uses them as a relish with the bread at the beginning and the end, even though he eats some in between without bread, they are exempted by the berachah of Hamotzi; and some say that even if he uses them as a relish with bread at the beginning and the end, since he eats some in between without bread, they are not exempted by the berachah of Hamotzi, because he did not make his meal's basis upon them for the purpose of using them as a relish with the bread, since he has something else to use as a relish. Therefore, in order to satisfy both views, the acharonim, may their memory be blessed, wrote: if one wishes to eat some of them with bread and some without bread, he should do the following — eat a little of them first without bread and recite a berachah over them, and afterward eat them either with bread or without bread. And this law applies only when one has made his meal's basis upon other things but wishes also to use a little fruit as a relish with the bread; but if he has truly made his meal's basis upon the fruit itself, to use it as a relish with the bread, then he should eat bread with the fruit first and not recite a berachah over the fruit, and afterward, even if he eats some of it without bread, he should likewise not recite a berachah — though it is good to be careful to use it as a relish with bread again at the end as well; see the acharonim, may their memory be blessed. Therefore, those who are accustomed in the summer to eat bread and cheese, but eat with them cucumbers or watermelons, making all their "relish" with the cheese, and only in between, after using two or three pieces of cheese as relish, take a piece of cucumber or watermelon without using it as a relish with bread, in order to sweeten their eating after the saltiness of the cheese — they must be careful to eat first from the cucumbers or watermelons with bread, and also at the end be careful to use them as a relish with bread; and then in between they may eat several pieces of them one after another without using bread as a relish. And the most correct thing to do is to eat one piece of them before netilat yadayim and recite a berachah with the intent to exempt whatever he will eat of them during the meal, and thus he eats of them during the meal without using bread as a relish, without any hesitation; see the acharonim.

clarification.explanation:
One who made his meal's basis upon something other than fruit, and fruits were also brought before him, and he eats some of them with bread and some without bread — there is a dispute about this: some say that as long as he uses them as a relish with the bread at the beginning and the end, even though he eats some in between without bread, they are exempted by the berachah of Hamotzi; and some say that even if he uses them as a relish with bread at the beginning and the end, since he eats some in between without bread, they are not exempted (since he did not make his meal's basis upon them). Therefore, to satisfy both views, the acharonim wrote: if one wishes to eat some of them with bread and some without, he should eat a little of them first without bread and recite a berachah over them first, and afterward eat them either with or without bread.
All this applies when one has made his meal's basis upon other things and merely wishes to also use a little fruit as a relish with bread; but if he has truly made his meal's basis upon the fruit itself, to use it as a relish with the bread — he should eat bread with the fruit first without reciting a berachah over the fruit (and it is good to also use it as a relish with bread again at the end). Therefore, those accustomed in the summer to eat bread and cheese together with cucumbers or watermelons, doing all their "relish" with the cheese, and only in between, between two or three pieces of cheese, taking a piece of cucumber or watermelon without using bread as a relish, to sweeten their eating from the saltiness of the cheese — must be careful to eat first from the cucumbers or watermelons with bread, and also be careful to use them as a relish with bread at the end; and the most correct practice is to eat a piece of them before netilat yadayim and recite a berachah with intent to exempt whatever he eats of them during the meal.
takeaways: One who made his meal's basis upon something else and eats fruit partly with bread and partly without — there is a dispute whether it is exempted by Hamotzi.
To resolve the doubt: eat a little of it without bread and recite the berachah first, and then eat as one wishes; or recite a berachah over a piece before netilat yadayim to exempt it.
One who made his meal's basis upon the fruit itself — should eat it with bread first without a berachah (and use it as a relish with bread again at the end).

paragraphs: Chesed LaAlafim writes in siman 177, ot 6: cooked fruits as such, even together with meat, if it was not the beginning of his making his meal's basis upon them — there is one who says that one must recite a berachah over them, and likewise regarding pickled cucumbers and the like; and there is one who says that even if one eats them with bread, one must recite a berachah; and there is one who says that one should not recite a berachah, since they come for the purpose of the meal and not for dessert. Therefore, one who fears Heaven should sit before the meal and recite a berachah over that type of fruit and eat less than the required measure, intending to exempt — thus far his words. And if this is not possible for him, particularly if he is a guest, he should then contemplate the berachah in his heart, or say "Blessed is the Merciful One, Creator of the fruit of the earth" or "Creator of the fruit of the tree," according to what the fruit is.

clarification.explanation: Cooked fruits as they are — even together with meat — if they were not present from the beginning of the meal's basis, there is one who says one must recite a berachah over them, and likewise regarding pickled cucumbers and the like; and there is one who says that even eating them with bread requires a berachah; and there is one who says one should not recite a berachah, since they come for the purpose of the meal and not for dessert (Chesed LaAlafim). Therefore one who fears Heaven should sit before the meal and recite a berachah over that type of fruit, and eat less than the required measure, intending to exempt. And if this is not possible for him — particularly if he is a guest — he should contemplate the berachah in his heart, or say "Blessed is the Merciful One, Creator of the fruit of the earth" or "Creator of the fruit of the tree," according to what the fruit is.
takeaways: Cooked or pickled fruits brought during the meal — there is a dispute whether one recites a berachah over them (even with bread).

One who fears Heaven should recite a berachah over them before the meal (less than the required measure) to exempt; and if not possible — contemplate it in his heart, or say "Blessed is the Merciful One, Creator of the fruit of the earth/tree."

paragraphs: At the Friday night meal, people are accustomed to linger at the table three or four hours, especially in the winter days, and their custom is as follows: after the berachah of Hamotzi they eat salted foods in vinegar, and they eat the meat dishes made in a pot which were cooked in honor of Shabbat, and afterward they remove the cooked dish and bring types of fruit and place them on the table and recite a berachah over them, and linger at the table two or three hours until they recite Birkat HaMazon. However, their custom is to leave bread on the table until Birkat HaMazon, so that it should appear that they have not yet withdrawn their hands from the bread — for if they had withdrawn their hands from the bread, they would need to recite a berachah over everything brought afterward, whether things that come on account of the meal, such as fish and the like, or types of fruit, which in my opinion require a berachah before and after them, since neither the berachah of Hamotzi nor Birkat HaMazon exempts them, as these were brought after they had withdrawn their hands from the bread. Therefore they are careful to leave a slice of bread on the table so that it appears they have not withdrawn their hands from the bread, and thus they are not seen as being negligent regarding berachot when they do not recite a berachah over these things. However, even though the bread remains on the table until Birkat HaMazon, one who fears Heaven should be careful to eat a little of the bread very close to the taking of the final water (mayim acharonim), and also at the time the fruits are arranged on the table he should likewise eat a little of the bread, so that it will truly be found that he has not withdrawn his hand from the bread. And in our own household it is our custom to bring fish also at the first and second Shabbat meals, and a little of it is eaten together with bread close to the taking of the final water, and this is a fine and correct custom, for thereby, throughout the two or three hours we sit at the table set with fruits, we do not withdraw our hands from the bread, since we intend to eat still more bread together with the fish eaten at the end.

clarification.explanation: At the Friday night meal it is customary to linger at the table for many hours: one eats salted foods in vinegar, meat dishes, and afterward the cooked dish is removed and fruits are brought. It became customary to leave a slice of bread on the table until Birkat HaMazon, so that it should appear one has not "withdrawn his hands from the bread" — for if one had withdrawn his hands, he would need to recite a berachah over everything brought afterward (both meal-items and fruit). Therefore, even though the bread remains on the table, one who fears Heaven should be careful to taste a little bread very close to the end, and likewise when the fruits are arranged on the table — so that he truly does not withdraw his hand from the bread.
takeaways: It is customary to leave bread on the table throughout the meal (as a sign that one's "hands were not withdrawn" from it).
It is good to taste a little bread very close to the end, so as to actually maintain the continuity of eating bread.

paragraphs: If one ate a cooked dish of cucumbers, or pickled cucumbers and the like, during the meal without reciting a berachah over it, and after the end of the meal, before Birkat HaMazon, fruits were arranged before him for dessert and enjoyment, and among them raw cucumbers were also brought, there are those who say that one must recite a berachah over them, and there are those who say that one need not recite a berachah. Therefore one who fears Heaven should eat another type whose berachah is the same as this type, and recite a berachah over it, thereby also exempting this one; or, before eating the cooked dish and the pickled item, he should take a piece of this type and not eat from it at that time, so as not to place himself in the dispute regarding berachot. But he has no remedy of saying he will eat and contemplate the berachah in his heart, for this is said only in a case of unavoidable circumstance and great difficulty — see Zechor LeYitzchak Harari, may his memory be blessed, siman 48 — see there. And if he can find another person to eat and recite a berachah and intend for him, behold how good that is!

clarification.explanation: One who ate, during the meal, a cooked dish of cucumbers or pickled cucumbers without reciting a berachah over them, and afterward (before Birkat HaMazon) fruits were brought to him for dessert, among them raw cucumbers — there is a dispute whether one must recite a berachah over them: some say yes, some say no. Therefore one who fears Heaven should follow one of two paths in order not to enter into doubt: eat another type whose berachah is identical to that of cucumbers and recite a berachah over it with intent to also exempt the cucumbers; or, before eating the cooked dish or the pickled item at the beginning of the meal, take for himself a piece of a raw cucumber and not eat it yet (so that it remains requiring a berachah later, and he does not enter into doubt). A third, even better way: if he can find another person who will eat some of those cucumbers and recite a berachah over them, intending to also exempt him — that is very good. One should not rely merely on contemplating the berachah in his heart, for that is resorted to only in a case of unavoidable circumstance and real difficulty.
takeaways: Raw cucumbers brought for dessert after cooked cucumbers were eaten without a berachah — there is a dispute whether they require a berachah.
The solution: recite a berachah over another type with an identical berachah, intending to exempt it as well; or set aside a piece of cucumber in advance and not eat it.
Another good option: find another person to eat and recite a berachah over the cucumbers, intending to exempt him too.

paragraphs: One who fears Heaven should be careful at every meal, at the time he recites a berachah, to have in mind everything that may come to him, even in an unlikely way that is not the ordinary course of things — because there are those who say that if, after he recited a berachah over the bread, others sent him a gift from their house and he did not have the gift in mind, then even if it is of the type ordinarily used as a relish with bread, nevertheless if he does not eat it with bread he must recite a berachah over it, as in the law of one who changes his mind; and there are those who say he need not recite a berachah, since a person's mind is ordinarily set on everything that will be brought to him at the meal. Therefore, one who is careful to have in mind, at the time he recites the berachah over the bread, the wine, and the fruit, everything that will be brought to him — whether as a gift, even from a distant place — is saved from this rock of dispute, and upon him will come a blessing of good.

clarification.explanation: One who fears Heaven should be careful at every meal, at the time he recites the berachah, to have his mind on everything that may come to him — even in a far-fetched way that is not usual. The reason: there are those who say that if, after he recited a berachah over the bread, a gift was sent to him from another's house and he had not had it in mind, then even if it is of the type ordinarily used as a relish with bread — if he does not eat it with bread, he must recite a berachah over it, in the law of one who changes his mind; and there are those who say he need not recite a berachah, since a person's mind is ordinarily set on everything brought to him at the meal. Therefore, one who is careful to have in mind, at the time he recites the berachah over the bread, the wine, and the fruit, everything that will be brought to him — even as a gift and from a distant place — is saved from this dispute, and blessing will come upon him.
takeaways: At the time of the berachah, intend everything that will come during the meal, even a gift arriving from far away.
A gift that arrives after the berachah, which was not intended — there is a dispute whether one must recite a berachah over it; one who intends everything in advance is saved from the doubt.
